Series::skewness¶

Back to Series::StatAccessor API Reference

Signature¶

Series::stat.skewness() -> Series
Series::stat.skewness(std::int64_t dim) -> Series
Series::stat().skewness() -> Series
Series::stat().skewness(std::int64_t dim) -> Series

What It Does¶

skewness() measures asymmetry.

At a high level:

  • positive skewness means a heavier or longer right tail

  • negative skewness means a heavier or longer left tail

  • zero skewness means the lane is symmetric around its center

Unlike center and standardize, this is a reduction again: one summary value per reduced lane.

Surface Note¶

On the current public surface documented here, use the stats accessor spelling:

  • x.stat.skewness(...)

  • x.stat().skewness(...)

That is the verified callable path used by the compiled examples below.

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t)

The reduced axis.

Important details:

  • omit dim to summarize the entire Series

  • pass dim to compute one skewness value per remaining lane

  • negative dims count from the back

Returns¶

Series A reduction result containing one skewness value per surviving lane, or one value for the entire Series when no dim is provided.

Gradient¶

This is primarily a descriptive higher-moment statistic. It is more useful for diagnostics and distribution understanding than for ordinary model plumbing.

Examples¶

The examples below move from symmetric lanes to lopsided ones, then compare lane-wise and global readings.

Example 1. Symmetric rows have zero skewness.

auto values = pluss::make_series(
    {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, {2, 3});

std::cout << values.stat.skewness(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0]

That is the expected result because [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6] are symmetric around their row means.

Example 2. The explicit proxy spelling stat().skewness(dim) reaches the same row-wise computation.

std::cout << values.stat().skewness(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0]

That is the same statistic as Example 1, reached through the more explicit accessor call form.

Example 3. Lopsided rows produce positive skewness.

auto lopsided = pluss::make_series(
    {1, 1, 4, 2, 2, 8}, {2, 3});

std::cout << lopsided.stat.skewness(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0.70710678, 0.70710678]

This is the page’s main practical lesson:

  • skewness is about shape, not just spread

  • two lanes can have similar variance but different asymmetry

Example 4. Global skewness can differ materially from per-row skewness because pooling changes the distribution you are summarizing.

std::cout << lopsided.stat.skewness();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[1.2247449]

Here the pooled distribution is more asymmetric than either individual row, so the global skewness is larger.

Example 5. Negative dimensions count from the back, so -1 means the last axis.

std::cout << lopsided.stat.skewness(-1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0.70710678, 0.70710678]

On this 2D shape, the last axis is the row axis, so the result matches Example 3.

Gotchas And Notes¶

  • Use the stat accessor path on this surface.

  • Zero skewness means symmetry, not “low variance.”

  • Positive skewness does not tell you the spread by itself; it tells you the direction of imbalance.

  • Very short lanes can still produce a skewness value, but you should interpret it carefully because a small number of points makes higher-moment summaries fragile.

  • A dim outside the valid axis range fails.

Summary¶

Use skewness() when you want to summarize distribution shape rather than transform values:

  • zero means symmetric around the center

  • positive means the right side is heavier or longer

  • negative means the left side is heavier or longer

  • global and lane-wise skewness can differ a lot because they summarize different distributions

See Also¶

  • Series::kurtosis: fourth-moment tail/peakedness summary.

  • Series::var: second-moment spread summary.
